titre: Music, a Universal Language: What Two Studies Measured
accroche: Music exists in all 315 societies studied. But listeners guessing the purpose of a foreign song are wrong more than half the time.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Music is the universal language of mankind”: the phrase has been repeated so often that it was long taken as self-evident, without being measured. Two large studies, one from 2015, the other from 2019, have done so. They confirm one half of the sentence and undo the other.

## What is everywhere

In 2019, Samuel Mehr and his colleagues first queried the ethnographies of 315 societies gathered in the eHRAF World Cultures database. They describe music in 309 of them. The other six (the Turkmen, the Dominicans, the Hazaras, the peoples of the Pamir, the Tajiks, and the Ghorbat) have it too, according to other firsthand ethnographic documents: music is present in 100% of the sample. In a subset of 60 societies, songs are described in all of them.

The researchers also gathered 118 field recordings from 86 societies, of four kinds: dance songs, lullabies, healing songs, and love songs. They looked for one of each kind in each of 30 large regions of the world, or 120 possible cases, and found 118. The two missing (healing songs in Scandinavia and the British Isles) existed, but had become rare by the time recording began. Another measure: of the 118 songs, 113 were judged tonal, that is, organized around a central note, by more than 90% of 30 expert listeners.

## What is not

A 2015 study, by Patrick Savage and his colleagues, had already analyzed 304 recordings from nine regions. No musical feature is present in all musics: there is no absolute universal. There are, however, 18 common features and a network of ten features that often go together, such as the tendency to sing, to play percussion, and to dance in a group to simple, repetitive music.

And a language is understood. In the 2019 online experiment, 29,357 people listened to excerpts drawn at random from the 118 songs and had to guess which of the four uses was the right one. They succeeded in 42.4% of cases, against 25% by chance: better than chance for each of the four types, far from a reliable understanding, and love songs are by far the most ambiguous. Another result that disturbs stereotypes: for three dimensions of musical behavior (formality, arousal, religiosity), the variation within a single society is about six times greater than between two societies.

## What this shifts

What is universal is not messages but situations: soothing a baby, dancing, healing, courting, and a tendency of form to fit these situations. A foreign song is not translated; at best, one guesses what it is for. Music looks less like a common language than like a family of uses that each society has filled in its own way. What remains is to explain why these situations, and not others, have everywhere called for song.

repere.texte: In an online experiment with 29,357 participants, listeners guessed the use of songs from around the world (dance, lullaby, healing, love) with a 42.4% success rate, against 25% by chance.
repere.source: Mehr et al., “Universality and diversity in human song,” Science, 2019

carte.punch: Music exists everywhere, but guessing the use of a foreign song works only 42% of the time
carte.idee: Music is present in all the societies studied, but it is not a language: 29,357 listeners guessed the use of songs from around the world (dance, lullaby, healing, love) in 42.4% of cases, against 25% by chance.

quiz.question: What does the 2019 online experiment on songs from around the world show?
choix: Listeners almost always identify the use of the song, as if music were a common language
Listeners fail: their answers do not exceed chance, which is 25%
Only lullabies are recognized, the other three uses remain at chance level
Listeners guess the use better than chance, but remain far from a reliable understanding
quiz.explication: With a 42.4% success rate against 25% by chance, the forms of songs do carry a trace of their use, but far too little to speak of a language. Listeners do not almost always succeed, they are not reduced to chance, and all four uses (dance, lullaby, healing, love) are identified above chance, not just lullabies.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Of the 315 societies studied by Mehr et al., how many have music according to the ethnographies alone?
choix: 118 societies, the number of recorded songs
309 societies, the other six confirmed by other documents
286 societies, about 90% of the total sample
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The ethnographies in the eHRAF database describe music in 309 of 315 societies; the remaining six have it too, according to other firsthand documents, bringing the total to 100%.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the corpus include only 118 songs out of the 120 cases the researchers aimed for?
choix: The two missing ones, healing songs, had become rare before recordings began
Two societies studied refused access to their ethnographic archives
No lullaby could be found in two regions of the world
Love songs were missing in two of the thirty regions studied
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The two songs missing from the 118-song corpus were healing songs, in Scandinavia and the British Isles, which had become rare by the time of the first recordings.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the study by Savage and his colleagues (2015) find across the 304 recordings analyzed?
choix: A single feature, regular rhythm, is present in all the world's musics
No common feature could be drawn out of the statistical analysis
The 304 recordings show an identical harmonic structure everywhere
No feature is present in all musics, but 18 are statistically common
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Savage et al. find no absolute musical universal, but 18 statistically common features and a network of ten features that often go together, such as singing and dancing in a group.
